analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA approve competing generic drugs when a first generic applicant sits on its exclusivity for 30 months.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill unanimously by voice vote in May 2019, but it sat on the House calendar for 20 months and never got a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker is first in line to copy a brand-name drug, the FDA gives it 180 days of market exclusivity as a reward. But that clock only starts when the company actually starts selling the drug, so some first applicants sit on their approval — sometimes for years — while cheaper copies are kept off the market. This bill says if a first applicant's application has been pending at least 30 months and patent lawsuits aren't blocking approval, the FDA can approve the next generic in line instead of letting one company lock up the market by doing nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay full brand-name prices for drugs where a generic has already been approved but is being held back by a first applicant parking its exclusivity. Every month a cheaper generic stays off the market, patients and insurers pay brand-name prices; this bill shortens those delays.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying brand-name prices for drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets the FDA approve a subsequent generic application before a first applicant has started selling, if the first applicant's application has been pending for at least 30 months and patent infringement claims are not precluding its approval.

It starts the first applicant's 180-day exclusivity clock at the earlier of first commercial marketing or the point when those 30-month conditions are met, so exclusivity can no longer be frozen indefinitely by not launching.

The bill preserves the first-filer reward where it is doing its intended job: approval of later generics is still blocked if patent claims preclude the first applicant's approval, keeping the incentive to challenge patents through litigation.

analysis.who_pays: First generic applicants who have been parking their 180-day exclusivity without launching lose the ability to keep competitors off the market indefinitely. Brand-name drug makers also lose, because more generic competition reaches the market sooner and puts downward pressure on their prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and generics firms

drawbacks.text: The 180-day exclusivity reward exists to pay a first applicant for the cost and risk of challenging a brand-name drug's patents; if a competitor can be approved after 30 months regardless, first filers have less reason to take on those court battles, which could slow generics in some cases. The bill tries to limit this by keeping the exclusivity shield wherever patent claims actually preclude approval [S2] [S3].

The bill is narrow: it only touches drugs where a first generic application has sat pending at least 30 months with no patent bar, so it addresses one specific gap in generic competition and does nothing about other drivers of high drug prices such as patent thickets or brand-name pricing itself [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but targeted: faster generic availability for the specific set of drugs where a first filer is parked, which means lower out-of-pocket costs for patients on those drugs. The trade-off — weakening the reward that motivates patent challenges — is a fair objection, but the bill's design protects the exclusivity reward in exactly the cases where patents are genuinely in dispute. On balance the benefits to patients exceed the costs, though the bill alone would not fix high drug prices broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it on a voice vote and placed it on the House calendar in May 2019, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Kurt Schrader introduced the bill on January 31, 2019, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

The Health Subcommittee forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote on March 27, 2019, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote on April 3 — voice votes meaning no member requested a recorded opposition vote.

The committee reported the bill on May 2, 2019, with a bipartisan group of 17 members including Chairman Frank Pallone (D-NJ) and Ranking Member Greg Walden (R-OR) signed on, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
The bill then sat on the calendar with no further action for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: First generic applicants that park their exclusivity and brand-name drug makers that benefit from delayed competition are better off, because the bill never became law and the status quo continued. Patients kept paying brand-name prices in the affected cases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Generics firms parking exclusivity, brand-name drug makers

industries.note: Sooner and broader generic competition means lower revenue on drugs where a first generic is approved but held back. Their interest in delaying generics runs directly against patients paying brand prices.

These firms could historically keep the 180-day exclusivity clock from starting by not launching, blocking later generics. The bill ends that hold-out strategy by starting the clock after 30 months of inactivity.
Later generic applicants can win FDA approval sooner instead of waiting behind a parked first filer, and their interest — getting cheaper copies to market — matches what patients want.
More available generics means lower acquisition and reimbursement costs for dispensers and plan sponsors, though the bill does not address them directly.
